name: Sleep habits education (sleep hygiene) - adjunct only
modality: Psychoeducation - sleep habits (complementary and integrative; adjunct)
evidenceLevel: Adjunct only. The AASM 2021 guideline suggests that clinicians not use sleep hygiene as a single-component therapy for chronic insomnia (conditional recommendation against). Multicomponent CBT-I, which may include sleep education, is strongly recommended (Edinger et al., 2021). The AASM patient guide notes that most people with chronic insomnia need more than basic sleep-hygiene advice, and NCCIH notes that the strongest evidence for chronic insomnia supports CBT-I.
purpose: Brief education about daily habits and the sleep setting that can support sleep: a regular rise time, daylight and activity during the day, less caffeine later in the day, avoiding alcohol and nicotine near bedtime, avoiding heavy meals late at night, a wind-down routine, a dark, quiet, comfortable room, and keeping screens and work out of bed. It is useful as general health information and as one part of CBT-I, but it is not an effective stand-alone treatment for chronic insomnia. When insomnia persists, offer CBT-I or refer for it.
steps: Ask about current habits using the sleep diary: caffeine, alcohol and nicotine timing, naps, exercise timing, screens, the bedroom, and work or caregiving schedules. Do not record substance-use details in this app.
Choose two or three changes the client is willing to try rather than handing over a long list of rules.
Explain each change in plain language and link it to the client's own diary (for example, late coffee and taking a long time to fall asleep).
Give the sleep-habits handout and agree on when you will review it.
Make clear that habits alone usually do not fix long-standing insomnia, and offer CBT-I (see cbti-stimulus-control and cbti-sleep-restriction) or a referral.
Screen for, and refer for medical evaluation of, signs of sleep apnea, restless legs or other sleep disorders, and medicines that may be affecting sleep.
Watch for 'trying too hard' to sleep. If the client becomes anxious about following rules perfectly, shift the focus to CBT-I and to accepting that some nights vary.
script: Small daily habits can help your sleep a bit. They are a good start, but often not the whole answer.
Let's pick two or three things to try, not ten.
Getting up at the same time every day helps set your body clock.
Try to get some daylight in the morning and move your body during the day.
Caffeine can stay in your body for many hours. Try to have it earlier in the day.
Alcohol may help you fall asleep, but it often wakes you up later in the night.
If your sleep problems keep going, there is a treatment called CBT for insomnia. It works better than tips alone.
contraindications: Do not use sleep hygiene as the only treatment for chronic insomnia (AASM 2021). Offer CBT-I or refer.
Rigid rules can raise anxiety about sleep. Keep advice flexible and focused on the client's chosen changes.

Alcohol: clients who drink heavily every day, or who have had withdrawal symptoms, need medical assessment before cutting down quickly, because alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous. Do not record substance-use details in this tool.
Exercise advice should respect medical limits. Check with the client's medical provider when there are heart, lung or mobility concerns.

Persistent insomnia with low mood, hopelessness or suicidal thoughts needs safety assessment. This tool does not judge risk. Crisis options: in the US, call or text 988; elsewhere, the local emergency number or findahelpline.com.
culturalAdaptations: Tea, coffee and other caffeinated drinks can be central to hospitality and daily life. Discuss timing and amount rather than asking the client to give them up.
Afternoon rest is valued in many cultures. Agree on a nap plan that respects this.
Shared rooms, noise and limited money for curtains or bedding are common. Suggest low-cost options and problem-solve with the client.
Night prayer, religious fasting and shift work shape sleep routines. Build advice around the client's schedule. Translate handouts or use a professional interpreter when needed.
